   - `risk_of_bias_tool`: Pick the single design-matched tool per `RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1:
     * `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"` (individually randomized trial)
     * `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"` (cluster-randomized trial — check unit of randomization carefully!)
     * `"ROBINS-I"` (non-randomized intervention / quasi-experimental study with a genuine comparator: DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, policy panel FE)
     * `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"` (quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without quasi-experimental intervention comparator)
     * `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"` (observational longitudinal cohort study without intervention framing)
     * `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"` (primary qualitative study: interviews, focus groups, ethnography, qualitative case study)
     * `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"` (genuine mixed-methods study combining both qualitative and quantitative primary components)
     * `"AMSTAR 2"` (systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with systematic search/screening; NEVER use for non-systematic narrative literature reviews)
     * `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"` (legal-empirical, doctrinal-empirical, jurimetric, or institutional-historical study that fits none of the six conventional designs above)
     * `"NONE"` (fits none of the listed tools, e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model, or non-systematic narrative review/essay without primary empirical data or systematic search — explain why in `comment`)
   - `mechanism_certainty`: Single integer `"0"`, `"1"`, `"2"`, `"3"`, or `"4"` strictly obeying `CODEBOOK.md` §9 and its design ceiling:
     * `"4"` ONLY for randomized trials (`RoB 2`)
     * `"3"` ONLY for `RoB 2` trials OR `ROBINS-I` studies with credible Low/Moderate overall risk of bias
     * All other designs (cross-sectional/JBI, cohort, qualitative/CASP, mixed-methods/MMAT, systematic review/AMSTAR 2, Legal Framework, NONE, or Serious/Critical ROBINS-I) CANNOT exceed `"2"`! (`"2"` = mechanism directly observed empirically; `"1"` = documented statistical/descriptive association; `"0"` = inferred only by authors).

country.comment: The study analyzes households across Africa merged with mining records across 28 African countries; the individual country list is placed in Appendix Table A-XIII (online Supporting Information, not printed in the 16-page main article PDF).
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 4, Section Data; PDF p. 6, Section Descriptive statistics

effect_estimate.comment: Note that minus signs in Tables 2, 3, and 4 were dropped in the Wiley PDF text layer, with coefficient signs explicitly confirmed in the Abstract, Figure 1, and main text (PDF pp. 1, 8, 10–13). Sample mean probability of going without clean water is 0.36 (SD 0.48).
effect_estimate.value: In 2SLS IV regressions (N = 142,838 households), active mining operations within a 0–50 km radius reduce the probability of a household going without clean water in the past 12 months by 3.6 percentage points (-0.036, SE = 0.005, p < 0.01; reported as ~4% lower probability in the Abstract; Kleibergen-Paap rk Wald F = 13.044), whereas mines within a 50–100 km radius increase the probability of going without clean water by 0.5 percentage points (+0.005, SE = 0.002, p < 0.01). Comparing operational status within 50 km via 2SLS (F = 7.716), active mines reduce water insecurity (-0.027, SE = 0.005, p < 0.01), while inactive (closed) mines have an imprecise positive estimate (+0.072, SE = 0.117, not statistically significant). Regarding local governance (LPM/OLS with country and year fixed effects, N = 142,838), a 1-unit worsening (1–4 scale) in regional perceived corruption of local councillors (+0.10, p < 0.01; +0.106, SE = 0.005 in Table 4), corruption of tax officials (+0.13, p < 0.01), and disapproval of local government (+0.05, p < 0.01) increases household water insecurity, and local councillor corruption significantly moderates the effects of both active mines within 50 km (interaction magnitude 0.035, SE = 0.004, p < 0.01) and non-active mines within 50 km (interaction +0.040, SE = 0.013, p < 0.05), such that water insecurity worsens under corrupt local governance after mine closure.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 8–10, Tables 2–3; PDF pp. 11–13, Figure 1 and Table 4

mechanism_certainty.comment: Although mine proximity is estimated with 2SLS IV (with weak-instrument F = 7.716 in the active/inactive split and potential exclusion-restriction concerns from co-located unregistered artisanal mining), the local institutional/governance analysis (regional perceptions of local councillor/tax official corruption and local government disapproval) relies on uninstrumented observational OLS/LPM regressions (Table 4) and tests statistical associations/interactions with self-reported water deprivation without directly observing administrative or regulatory enforcement mechanisms.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 4; PDF pp. 7–13, Empirical strategy, Figure 1, and Tables 2–4; PDF p. 14, Conclusions

mechanism_flags.comment: No specific CODEBOOK.md §4 legal/administrative last-mile water-access mechanism codes are empirically examined. The paper analyzes spatial proximity to active/inactive registered mines and broad regional perception scores of local government corruption (local councillors, tax officials) and general local government disapproval, while mentioning environmental regulation enforcement and monitoring only generically in discussion.
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 4–7, Table 1; PDF pp. 10–14, Section The Relevance of Local Governance for the Effects of Mining and Conclusions

outcome_flags.comment: Measured via a binary indicator of self-reported clean water deprivation derived from Afrobarometer ('Over the past year, how often, if ever, have you or anyone in your family: Gone without enough clean water for home use?', coded 1 if experienced at least once in the past 12 months and 0 if never). Community piped water is included only as a control variable, and sanitation is not measured.

sample_size.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 4, Section Data; PDF pp. 9–10, Tables 2–3; PDF p. 12, Table 4

study_design.comment: Combines repeated cross-sectional geo-referenced Afrobarometer household survey waves (2005–2015) with spatial buffers (0–50 km and 50–100 km) around geo-coded active and inactive commercial mines; causal effects of mining are estimated via 2SLS IV (and Logit robustness in online Appendix Table A-X), while local institutional quality main and interaction effects are estimated via LPM/OLS with country and year fixed effects.
study_design.value: Repeated cross-sectional spatial econometric study using Linear Probability Models (LPM) and Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS) instrumental variable regressions (instrumenting active and inactive mines within 0–50 km and 50–100 km with USGS nonfuel mineral deposits) with country and year fixed effects, plus OLS interaction models for local institutional quality
